title: Spine with a fan
caption: A spine running from the problem (how do neurons combine signals?) through a method built to answer it (PID), into a fan of empirical findings about where synergy lives, and out to the method's limits and what comes next.

scenes.title: From the problem to the payoff

items.text: Brains process information — but how?
items.detail: New recording tech and new analysis tools now make this question tractable.

items.text: Mutual information vs. transfer entropy
items.detail: Mutual information shows undirected similarity between neurons; transfer entropy shows directed information flow from one to another.

items.text: But flow alone can't show how inputs combine
items.detail: Transfer entropy tracks propagation, not how a neuron integrates multiple sources into a new signal.

items.text: PID: split joint information into redundant, unique, synergistic parts
items.detail: Partial information decomposition formally separates overlapping, individual, and combination-only information.

items.text: Needs a choice of redundancy measure — none is universal
items.detail: The decomposition is underdetermined until one defines redundancy; a dozen competing definitions exist.

items.text: Applying PID to real recordings
items.detail: Hundreds of cultured cortical neurons, decomposed triad by triad, reveal where synergy concentrates.

items.text: Rich-club neurons hold most of the network's synergy
items.detail: A minority of best-connected neurons account for about 88% of all synergy.

items.text: Recurrent connections raise synergy; feedback doesn't
items.detail: Loops between source neurons add to synergy; feedback to the sources mostly doesn't.

items.text: Synergy peaks, then falls, as inputs grow more alike
items.detail: Mildly correlated sources produce the most synergy; highly correlated ones become redundant instead.

items.text: In monkeys, redundancy rises during movement
items.detail: Behaving-animal recordings show the balance of synergy and redundancy shifts with the task at hand.

items.text: Practical limits: data type, sample size, software tools
items.detail: Choosing a redundancy function and gathering enough data are both real constraints in practice.

items.text: Future: moment-by-moment and multi-target PID
items.detail: Local PID resolves synergy over time; integrated information decomposition extends it to multiple targets.

items.text: Synergy: neurons compute on patterns, not just totals
items.detail: The closing summary ties the empirical findings back to what synergy means for neural computation.

scenes.caption: Down the page is the article's own order: motivation, tools, the gap those tools leave, the PID framework built to fill it, a fan of empirical discoveries about synergy, then the method's limits, its future, and a closing summary.

scenes.title: Inside: building partial information decomposition

items.text: Joint information isn't just the sum of each source's part
items.detail: Summing each parent neuron's individual information about the target doesn't equal the information from all of them together.

items.text: Whole > parts means synergy; whole < parts means redundancy
items.detail: Extra information beyond the sum signals genuine integration (synergy); a shortfall signals double-counted overlap (redundancy).

items.text: Williams & Beer found how to split it algebraically
items.detail: Their partial information decomposition framework made this split exact, not just descriptive.

items.text: Two parents: redundant + unique(1) + unique(2) + synergistic
items.detail: With two source neurons, the joint information splits into four distinct, non-overlapping pieces.

items.text: Underdetermined — pick one piece to define
items.detail: Three known mutual-information values but four unknown pieces: defining any one term yields the rest.

items.text: More than two parents: need the partial information lattice
items.detail: With three or more sources the simple algebra isn't enough; a structured lattice of all possible source combinations is required.

items.text: Lattice atoms computed by Möbius inversion
items.detail: A recursive formula extracts each unique information atom once a redundancy measure is chosen.

scenes.caption: A chain of logical steps: the discovery that information doesn't simply add up, the algebra that first split it into parts for two sources, and the lattice machinery needed once there are more than two — all resting on one still-unsettled choice, the definition of redundancy.

scenes.title: Inside: what PID found in real circuits

items.text: 512-channel recordings from cultured mouse cortex
items.detail: Hundreds of neurons recorded at once, with thousands of source-source-target triads analyzed by PID.

items.text: Synergy tracks the strength of feedforward information flow
items.detail: Across 25 recordings, synergy was reliably about a quarter of the feedforward transfer entropy.

items.text: Rich-club triads: 2.7x more synergy, ~88% of total
items.detail: Densely interconnected 'rich club' neurons are small in number but dominant in synergy.

items.text: Recurrent links help synergy; feedback links don't
items.detail: Connections between source neurons raised synergy; connections back from target to sources mostly didn't.

items.text: Synergy peaks then falls as sources grow more alike
items.detail: Mild similarity between source neurons boosts synergy; too much similarity turns it into redundancy instead.

items.text: Caveats: bias from simple pairwise flow estimates; culture, not living brain
items.detail: Results depend on bivariate transfer-entropy networks and on in-vitro cortical cultures, not behaving animals.

items.text: In behaving monkeys, redundancy rises during movement execution
items.detail: Task demands shift the balance: redundancy increases when reliable transmission to distant muscles matters most.

scenes.caption: A chain into a fan and back: recordings feed one overall finding (synergy tracks feedforward flow), which splits into three parallel discoveries about where and why synergy concentrates, which converge on caveats and then on a result from behaving animals.
